case_analysis.focal_point: Whether EPA’s denials of Renewable Fuel Standard “small refinery exemption” (SRE) petitions are the kind of EPA “action” that must be reviewed exclusively in the D.C. Circuit as “nationally applicable” (or as based on a published “nationwide scope or effect” finding), or instead must be reviewed in the appropriate regional circuit under Clean Air Act § 307(b)(1).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Clean Air Act, 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1) (judicial review venue for EPA actions; D.C. Circuit for nationally applicable actions or those based on a determination of nationwide scope/effect with a published finding; otherwise the appropriate regional circuit).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: EPA argues that the challenged SRE denials should be funneled to the D.C. Circuit because they are effectively nationwide in character: EPA applied a uniform, nationwide legal interpretation/policy governing SREs (including how to assess “disproportionate economic hardship”), so the action’s applicability/effect is not merely local to an individual refinery; allowing regional-circuit review invites forum shopping and risks conflicting rulings on a single national RFS program, and § 7607(b)(1) is designed to centralize review of such nationally significant EPA actions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The small refinery respondents contend that SRE denials are classic locally/regionally applicable adjudications: each denial resolves a refinery-specific hardship petition based on that refinery’s facts and circumstances, so § 7607(b)(1) requires review in the ‘appropriate circuit’ (here, the Fifth Circuit) unless EPA makes—and publishes—the statute’s required finding that the action is based on a determination of nationwide scope or effect; respondents argue EPA cannot re-label individualized decisions as national to evade regional review, and Congress deliberately guaranteed local circuit review for local actions.

Circuit could avoid inconsistent circuit law and forum shopping. Justice Thomas’s observation that Texas v. EPA’s broader “legal impact” phrasing is not necessary to its holding supports a minimalist path: enforce the statute’s text and the published-finding condition without importing an extra-textual uniformity test. Harrison v. PPG, as Justice Alito notes, concerns what counts as “final action” and does not authorize collapsing Congress’s venue categories or relaxing the publication prerequisite.

PPG Industries reinforces that precedent speaks to what counts as “final action,” not to collapsing Congress’s separate venue categories or excusing the published-finding prerequisite. Texas v. EPA’s “legal impact” phrasing cannot override the statute’s clear, proceduralized exception without letting agencies rewrite venue through litigation characterization.

Justice Thomas’s focus on the statute’s express “finds and publishes” prerequisite matters to me methodologically: allowing a generalized nationwide-policy rationale to substitute for that contemporaneous, public finding would erase Congress’s notice-and-fairness safeguard and, in practice, disadvantage smaller entities and affected communities by forcing distant, centralized litigation without the trigger Congress required. Small-refinery hardship exemptions are refinery-specific adjudications turning on individualized facts and local impacts, so they fit the statute’s local/regional category, and EPA cannot convert them into D.C.-only cases merely by arguing they reflect broader programmatic policy. Reading “nationally applicable” to swallow individualized exemption decisions would undermine access to justice for smaller entities by forcing distant, centralized litigation and would dilute Congress’s express publication safeguard for nationwide-scope channeling. That interpretation respects the statutory text and structure of § 7607(b)(1) and preserves fair, practical review in the circuits where the affected facilities operate.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 307(b)(1) sets a clear venue split: “nationally applicable” final actions go only to the D.C. Circuit, while “locally or regionally applicable” actions go to the “appropriate circuit,” unless EPA makes and publishes a contemporaneous “nationwide scope or effect” finding. 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1). Small-refinery hardship exemptions are, by their terms and operation, refinery-specific adjudications directed to a particular facility, and EPA’s policy-level interests in uniformity cannot override Congress’s textual requirement that the nationwide-scope exception depends on a published finding. Harrison v. PPG Industries, Inc., 446 U.S. 578 (1980), underscores that § 307(b)(1) is a venue-allocation rule Congress designed to channel national actions to the D.C. Circuit while preserving regional-circuit review for localized decisions. A workable middle-ground is to respect that text: individualized exemption grants/denials belong in the appropriate regional circuit, while EPA can secure D.C. Circuit review when it actually issues a nationally applicable rule or makes the statute’s published nationwide-scope finding.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 307(b)(1) draws a textual line: “nationally applicable” actions go to the D.C. Circuit, while “locally or regionally applicable” actions go to the “appropriate circuit” unless—and only unless—the Administrator both (1) finds the action is “based on a determination of nationwide scope or effect” and (2) “finds and publishes” that finding. 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1). Small-refinery hardship exemptions are refinery-specific adjudications directed to a single facility, so they fit the ordinary meaning of “locally or regionally applicable,” and EPA cannot convert them into D.C.-Circuit-only cases by pointing to downstream programmatic consequences rather than satisfying the statute’s express publication prerequisite. To the extent EPA relies on a “legal effect” gloss to treat these individualized decisions as “nationally applicable,” that approach is not compelled by the statute’s text and, in any event, Texas v. EPA (2016) contains dicta on that point because the parties there agreed the action was locally/regionally applicable. Enforcing Congress’s venue allocation as written also respects separation of powers by preventing agency-driven centralization of judicial review beyond what § 7607(b)(1) permits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 307(b)(1) channels review to the regional circuits for “any … locally or regionally applicable” final action, and it sends such an action to the D.C. Circuit only if EPA both (i) determines the action is “based on a determination of nationwide scope or effect” and (ii) “finds and publishes” that determination. 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1). Small-refinery hardship exemptions are refinery-specific adjudications, so they are best characterized as locally/regionally applicable actions; treating them as “nationally applicable” would dilute the statute’s careful venue line and invite EPA to centralize review without satisfying the statute’s express publication prerequisite. Consistent with judicial restraint and workability, the better reading adheres to the text’s action-by-action categorization and preserves the exception only when EPA contemporaneously makes and publishes the required nationwide-scope finding, rather than relying on broad programmatic consequences to override the regional-venue rule.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 307(b)(1) draws a textual line: “nationally applicable” EPA actions are reviewable only in the D.C. Circuit, while “locally or regionally applicable” actions “may be filed only in” the “appropriate circuit,” with a narrow exception when the action is “based on a determination of nationwide scope or effect” and the Administrator contemporaneously “finds and publishes” that fact. 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1). A small-refinery hardship exemption decision is refinery-specific and factbound, so it is “locally or regionally applicable” by its terms, and EPA’s policy interest in uniformity cannot override Congress’s venue allocation absent satisfaction of the statute’s express finding-and-publication predicates. Consistent with Texas v. EPA, 829 F.3d 405 (5th Cir. 2016), courts—not EPA—determine applicability and whether the published nationwide-scope finding requirement has been met, and the record as described does not show the Administrator made and published the requisite finding for these individualized determinations.
